name: Magnet therapy

lead: Magnet therapy is the practice of wearing or sleeping on permanent magnets, in bracelets, insoles, knee and back straps, pillows or mattress pads. Wearers use it chiefly for comfort: easing joint and muscle pain, supporting sleep and circulation. Some also link it to a fresher complexion, energy and a more youthful look, drawing on a long folk tradition of magnets as vitality aids.

The appearance payoff is mostly indirect and claimed: better sleep and less pain are said to show up as a rested face and easier movement. Researchers have run many placebo-controlled trials of static magnets for pain, with mixed and mostly small-effect results, and reviews report that the field strength of consumer magnets is too weak to change blood flow in tissue.

paras: Users wear magnetic bracelets, anklets or insoles, strap magnet pads over a sore joint, or use magnet-embedded pillows and mattress toppers, usually continuously over weeks. Products vary in magnet strength and in how the poles are arranged. Some people combine them with other recovery habits.

The magnets themselves are generally regarded as low risk. They can interfere with pacemakers, insulin pumps and implanted defibrillators, and they affect MRI safety. Reviewers note the main practical risks are cost and delaying proper diagnosis or treatment of a medical problem. In the US, the FDA does not permit magnet products to be marketed with unsubstantiated medical claims.

angle.text: Wearers use magnets for comfort and sleep, and proponents link these to a rested, more vital appearance. The link to looks is an inference by users rather than a measured outcome.

lead: Magnet therapy, also called magnetotherapy, is the application of static magnetic fields from permanent magnets to the body. Products include bracelets, jewelry, wrist, knee and back straps, insoles, pillows, blankets and mattress pads, most using ferrite or neodymium magnets [1][2].

People use it mainly to feel more comfortable: less joint and muscle pain, better sleep, warmer extremities. In appearance terms the chain is indirect and claimed: easing pain and improving rest are said to support a more rested look and easier posture and movement. Folk traditions also credit magnets with promoting youthful vigour and healthy circulation, an idea that circulates in wellness marketing [1][1].

Researchers have tested static magnets in trials for conditions such as osteoarthritis, carpal tunnel syndrome and low back pain. Reviews generally describe the results as inconclusive, with concerns about blinding, since magnets can be detected by their attraction to metal [2][3]. A related but distinct technology, pulsed electromagnetic field therapy, uses powered devices and is cleared by regulators for some medical uses [1].

Over US$1 billion yearly worldwide (2006 estimate) [2]

paras: Static magnet therapy uses permanent magnets whose field does not change over time. Consumer products typically produce fields of a few hundred to a few thousand gauss at the magnet surface, and the field falls off quickly with distance [2][1]. Different manufacturers assign different effects to the north and south poles or to alternating pole arrangements [2].
Besides wearables, the market has included creams, supplements, patches and 'magnetized' water [2].

Accounts of magnet use for healing reach back to antiquity: lodestones are described in ancient Egyptian, Chinese and Greek traditions, and Paracelsus promoted them in the 16th century [1]. In the 1770s Franz Anton Mesmer used magnets in his theory of 'animal magnetism', which a 1784 French royal commission attributed to imagination rather than a magnetic fluid [1].

Magnetic insoles and belts were sold in the 19th century, and a modern consumer industry grew in the late 20th century. A 2006 estimate put worldwide sales above US$1 billion a year, about US$300 million of it in the United States [2].

The most common claim is that magnets increase blood flow to the tissue beneath them. Reviewers state that hemoglobin is only weakly magnetic and that the fields of consumer magnets are far too weak to alter blood flow, and an early study of static fields up to 1 tesla found no change in local blood flow [2]. Some practitioners describe instead a balance of the body's 'energy', a concept not used in conventional medicine [2].

Randomized trials have compared real magnets with sham magnets for several conditions. A pilot trial in chronic low back pain used bipolar permanent magnets [4]; a double-blind pilot study examined static magnets for knee osteoarthritis [5]; and trials in carpal tunnel syndrome examined wrist magnets, including a 2018 randomized trial in 22 patients who wore high- or low-dose magnetic wristbands for six weeks [6][7]. A randomized pilot study also measured finger skin blood perfusion during exposure to a rare-earth magnet [8].

Narrative reviews of complementary therapies for osteoarthritis rated the evidence for magnet therapy as weak or contradictory [9], and a 2008 systematic review found insufficient evidence for pain relief [2]. A BMJ editorial in 2006 discussed the difficulty of blinding magnet trials and the effect this can have on results [10]. No trials have tested magnets for skin appearance or visible aging.

Static magnets are generally considered safe in themselves. Reviews identify the main risks as cost and delayed or avoided medical treatment, and advise that people with pacemakers, insulin pumps or similar devices not use them [2]. Magnetic items must be removed before MRI.

US FDA regulations do not allow magnet therapy products to be marketed with medical claims lacking substantiation [2]. The American Cancer Society states that available scientific evidence does not support claims for magnets in cancer or other treatments [2]. A 2002 National Science Foundation survey found only 25% of respondents who had heard of magnet therapy considered it 'not at all scientific' [2].
